title: AVA and the Courts: What Can We Learn from Alaska's Bold Experiment with Artificial Intelligence? — Court Leader's Advantage (NACM)
pub: Court Leader's Advantage podcast (National Association for Court Management) — moderated by Roger Rand (NACM Vice President), hosted by Peter Kiefer
author: Jeannie Sato · Aubrie Souza · Tom Martin · Roger Rand

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The AVA case accepts the cluster’s core proposition and materially extends it with an operational court example: bounded deployment depended on curated source material, layered controls, user testing, multidisciplinary work, continuing verification, and sustained staffing and funding. It demonstrates concretely why AI value comes from service and workflow redesign rather than stand-alone tool procurement.
qs: You can't automate a process if you don't have a process already.
We've learned, and we realize with future projects, it really isn't building a project, it's creating a new service that will need ongoing maintenance and ongoing staff dedicated time.

kp.k: AVA offers conversational access to court probate information
kp.d: The episode introduces AVA as having launched the previous month. Jeannie Sato describes its purpose as helping court users find relevant self-help information, particularly on mobile phones, rather than requiring them to navigate the Alaska Court System's over 220 self-help webpages across about a dozen case-type areas. Its initial scope is probate; Tom Martin also reports voice questions and read-aloud responses as accessibility features. These are intended service benefits, not measured access-to-justice outcomes.
qs: Last month, the state released the Alaska Virtual Assistant (AVA), an AI chatbot designed to help court users navigate the probate court system.
The Alaska Court system has over 220 web pages on self-help content in about a dozen different case type areas
One thing we didn't mention is that people can actually ask a question by just talking to AVA, or they can click a button to have it read aloud to them.

kp.k: Retrieval grounds answers in a curated legal knowledge base
kp.d: Martin explains that AVA uses retrieval augmented generation to locate and synthesize relevant source material. Sato says the team copied court webpage content into a separate knowledge base rather than having AVA retrieve directly from live webpages. Limiting answers to that material reflected the court's low tolerance for harm to users.
qs: We use Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), which is a way of connecting an AI to source documents, then having it find the most relevant information, synthesize it, then provide it back to the user.
We took all that content and basically copied it onto something that we called our knowledge base.
We only wanted AVA to give information that was in the knowledge base because our overriding concern was doing no harm

kp.k: Development exceeded initial funding and relied on donated labour
kp.d: Souza says grant-funded development was initially envisaged as about four months, with courts responsible for subsequent sustainability funding if successful. She states the original funding was insufficient. Martin says the budget reflected that four-month expectation and that he personally supplied the balance of the work, over a year, without additional funding. His comparison of nine months to a year for similar projects is based on his customer experience, not a reported industry study.
qs: Part of the application and selection criteria was the understanding that if we were successful, the court would then be responsible for funding going forward to sustain the project.
It was originally imagined to be about a four- month project.

My experience with a lot of different customers and a lot of different organizations, legal aid, state courts, is that the average is around nine months, and sometimes nine months to a year to complete.
So the balance of the time, over a year, was completely done by me, on my dime.
I did not seek, nor did I get any additional funding to do that.

kp.k: Expert testing iteratively checked answers against court information
kp.d: Sato reports that she and nine other Alaska team members initially developed 91 probate questions, recorded AVA's responses, checked them against the knowledge base, and supplied feedback for revisions. After about two rounds, they concentrated on 15 questions combining prior errors, common questions and difficult Alaska-specific issues, then returned to the 91-question set before launch. Alaska Legal Services Corporation was also asked to involve probate attorneys and staff, and clients where possible; the transcript does not establish how much client participation occurred.
qs: we came up with 91 questions that we thought users might ask over a variety of topics related to probate estates.

We switched to 15 questions and we chose some that AVA had answered incorrectly in the past, some that we thought were pretty common that a lot of people would ask, and some that we thought were pretty tricky and very Alaska-specific.
We went back and did the 91 again.
we gave them the link to AVA and asked them to have their probate attorneys and staff go through and ask some questions work through with some clients if they had the opportunity

kp.k: Layperson testing exposed comprehension gaps experts had missed
kp.d: Souza describes scenario-based, think-aloud testing with seven friends, relatives and neighbours rather than real users experiencing probate cases. Testers were asked to explain their next step in their own words. One believed they needed to obtain a personal representative despite occupying that role in the scenario. Souza says this prompted substantial changes to definitions and answer presentation, illustrating that perceived actionability could coexist with misunderstanding.
qs: While we weren't going to test with real court users experiencing a probate case, we wanted to make sure that it was used and tested by people without that background.
as they tried out AVA, we asked them to think out loud, tell us how they were understanding it, how they were forming their next question
They did not understand their role in a probate case.
it also led us to significant changes in how we were going to shape answers when definitions are provided, how we let people know they can ask for definitions if they don't understand it.
with only seven individuals, we were able to find those holes that we needed to address before launching.

kp.k: Testing identified unsupported and locally inappropriate answers
kp.d: Sato recounts AVA recommending a local law school's alumni association although Alaska has no law school, and using 'summary administration proceedings' rather than the locally used 'small estates'. The latter terminology had a statutory basis but was absent from the supplied court materials, so it should not be treated as equivalent to a fabricated statute. Martin attributes problematic answers to fabrication, pretrained knowledge and attempts to bridge gaps in source material. Despite the moderator asking how often errors occurred, the panel supplies examples rather than a numerical error rate.
qs: AVA answered, “You could check with your local law school's alumni association,” but Alaska is the only state without a law school.
And that statute is actually titled Summary Administration: Small Estates.
Everyone in Alaska calls them small estates. We put that on the forms. The judges and lawyers say small estates.
It hasn't searched the web, but it remembers this and it brings it up because it thinks it's being helpful.
it's trying to connect the dots between two separate concepts that is presented in the source documents where there is some kind of gap.

kp.k: Model selection and controls prioritize restraint over apparent intelligence
kp.d: Martin argues that the newest model is not necessarily appropriate for court information because its tendency to infer connections may conflict with the court's requirements. He describes combining model selection, prompt engineering, programming restrictions on web access and constraints favouring source documents over pretrained knowledge. He presents the desired behaviour as careful and rule-following, explicitly not acting as a lawyer; these are design claims, not evidence that all errors have been eliminated.
qs: a lot of people make the mistake of thinking, “oh, well just choose the latest, greatest model, Gemini three Pro, or Claude.”
you want it to be basically, the kind of persona of a lawyer, not acting as a lawyer, but have the same traits, rule following, careful, measured in what they can do and what they can't do.
Some of that is covered by prompt engineering, which Aubrie helped in detail with, to put limits on what the chatbot could talk about.
there's some behind-the-scenes, actual programming that we do to prevent it from accessing the web, to prevent it from relying on anything other than source documents.

kp.k: Preparing legal content required substantial specialist human work
kp.d: Sato says existing FAQ-style webpages at an eighth-ish grade reading level did not automatically constitute a usable AI knowledge base. The team paused for about two or three months while Souza and three court attorneys helped revise a 112-page document. They made implicit webpage context explicit, for example distinguishing identical questions about starting formal and informal probate cases. Martin argues that source material close to the intended lay answer reduces the need for model inference.
qs: the formatting that makes a good webpage, does not always make a good knowledge base for a large language model.
We did take about a two or three-month break.
We worked really hard with Aubrie and three attorneys on our staff
They were the exact same question, two places in the knowledge base with different answers.
And that's just one simple example of dozens and dozens and dozens of edits we made over this 112 page document.
the closer it is to each other, the less likely that AI is going to try to connect the dots because it doesn't have to.

kp.k: Participants frame extended development as necessary quality assurance
kp.d: The host frames the launch in terms of delays and sceptical coverage, while Martin and Souza contest the implication that the time taken represented failure. They attribute it to testing, coordination, content preparation and Alaska's particularly conservative risk tolerance. Sato likewise identifies avoiding harm as a reason for the time spent. This is the project participants' interpretation of the development process, not an independent assessment of its efficiency.
qs: I want to reject the premise of the question of it being delayed significantly.
It went into a lot of testing, the original 91 questions, those take time.
One part that people, I think, discount at the beginning, is the amount of time it takes to organize the information
With the court system, the risk profiles, is much more conservative for obvious reasons.
we can call it a delay, we can say it didn't go smoothly, but I think it was appropriate for a project that the goal was to provide legal information to court users.

kp.k: Court AI creates an ongoing service and staffing commitment
kp.d: Sato describes a dashboard allowing court staff to inspect every question and answer, with a continuing channel to Martin for concerns; Martin also describes a ticketing system and platform updates. The court plans at least six months to a year of monitoring and refinement before considering expansion beyond probate. Sato's central lesson is that a chatbot requires continuing maintenance and dedicated staff time, rather than ending at deployment. The described monitoring is post-response oversight, not prepublication human checking of each answer.
qs: we can see every question that anyone has asked AVA and get every answer.
That helps us to be looking at what's coming in, what kind of questions are happening, and then confirm AVA's giving information we're comfortable with.
we think we'll probably go at least six months to a year just really monitoring AVA and watching it grow and fine tune it before we would think about expanding it to any other areas
it really isn't building a project, it's creating a new service that will need ongoing maintenance and ongoing staff dedicated time.

kp.k: AI depends on established processes and interdisciplinary collaboration
kp.d: Souza describes translating between court procedure and technical implementation, checking legal accuracy and helping shape prompts. Martin emphasizes trust, collaboration and commitment to quality. Souza's broader recommendation is that courts must continue developing reliable processes and legal information: AI cannot bypass that foundational work, and Alaska's pre-existing content materially supported the project.
qs: I often describe my role as the translator between the courts and the technical

In this project, that meant for me diving both into the legal information, evaluating the results for accuracy, but then also working to structure some of the prompting and the technical choices that we made in the background.
One is that working with people you trust is immensely important.
The third thing is the vision of a commitment to quality.
You can't automate a process if you don't have a process already.
If we didn't have the robust information that Alaska already had, we would not have been able to turn it into the chatbot would've taken us much longer

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Sato and Martin describe conversational AI as a way to make court self-help information easier and faster to find, rather than requiring users to navigate extensive webpages.
pts.d: Jeannie Sato presents improved navigation as AVA's intended benefit, especially for mobile users. Tom Martin explains that retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant source information, synthesizes it and answers users' questions directly. This is a public-facing legal-information service focused on Alaska probate estates, not a claim that AI replaces lawyers or adjudicates cases. Martin also reports that voice input and read-aloud functions are intended to broaden access. The transcript offers no measured improvement in access to justice, completion rates or time saved.

pts.k: Martin and Sato claim that reliable court chatbots require deliberate restrictions and model selection; a newer or more capable model is not necessarily better suited to delivering bounded legal information.
pts.d: Sato reports that AVA initially supplied information outside the intended knowledge base, including inappropriate local-law-school advice and unfamiliar terminology for Alaska small estates. Martin distinguishes outright fabrication from drawing on training information and filling gaps between source concepts. Those latter problems are not necessarily fabricated facts: Sato found that 'Summary Administration: Small Estates' was an actual statutory title. Martin says source restrictions, prompting, programming and model choice help control these behaviors. He describes reliability improvements, not a quantified error rate or demonstrated elimination of hallucinations.

pts.k: Sato, Souza and Martin argue that AI does not eliminate the underlying work of preparing legal information and designing service processes.
pts.d: Sato says material that worked as public-facing webpages did not automatically work as a chatbot knowledge base. The team spent two or three months revising a 112-page document, including making formal and informal probate questions explicit. Martin argues that source material should closely match the desired layperson-facing answer to reduce the need for the model to infer connections. Aubrie Souza generalizes the lesson: existing processes and robust legal information remain prerequisites, and courts lacking them should expect more work. These claims are grounded in the project's development experience rather than comparative implementation research.

pts.k: Souza claims that testing with non-experts exposes comprehension and actionability problems that expert legal testing can miss.
pts.d: Souza reports that seven friends-and-family testers used realistic probate scenarios. One believed they needed to obtain a personal representative despite occupying that role in the scenario. The team consequently changed how answers handled definitions and encouraged clarification. The claimed benefit is better service design for lay users, not proof that AVA improved actual litigants' legal outcomes.

pts.k: Sato and Martin describe court AI as an ongoing, resource-intensive service rather than a one-off software build.
pts.d: Souza says the original four-month funding assumption was insufficient. Martin attributes development time to testing, coordination, information preparation and organizational risk tolerance, and reports contributing unpaid work beyond the funded scope. Sato says courts must dedicate continuing staff time and maintenance resources. Monitoring uses a dashboard showing questions and answers, with concerns referred to the vendor. This is ongoing human review of a public-facing service; the transcript does not say every answer is checked before users receive it.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is principally firsthand implementation experience, iterative internal testing and small-scale usability testing, rather than published performance metrics.
pts.d: Sato describes an initial 91-question test set, a reduced set of 15 recurring, difficult or previously mishandled questions, and a return to the full set before launch. Alaska Legal Services Corporation was invited to provide attorney and staff feedback, including possible client involvement; the transcript does not establish that clients participated. Souza explicitly describes the separate non-expert exercise as scenario testing rather than testing with people experiencing actual probate cases. Martin draws on his vendor experience to estimate typical development times. No numerical final accuracy, hallucination rate, independent benchmark, post-launch outcome study or quantified cost-benefit analysis is supplied. The speakers are project participants, with Martin also representing the technology supplier.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern an early-2026 launch and an extended development process; broader expansion is conditional on sustained monitoring and refinement.
pts.d: In this February 17, 2026 episode, participants describe a newly launched service. The original development estimate was about four months; Martin contrasts this with his experience of nine months to a year and reports over a year of additional volunteered time. The transcript does not provide a precise start-to-launch chronology. Sato anticipates at least six months to a year of monitoring before considering additional subject areas and says there are no current expansion plans. Reliability and implementation speed are explicitly qualified by knowledge-base quality, testing, technical controls and the court's conservative risk tolerance. Sustainability requires court funding after development.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The primary affected groups are self-represented probate users and the court staff, legal-information experts and vendors responsible for serving them.
pts.d: Alaska probate users are intended to receive more accessible, actionable information, including mobile and voice access, but may misunderstand legal roles or receive unsuitable information without careful design. Court access-to-justice staff and attorneys undertake testing, knowledge-base revision and ongoing review; NCSC supplies legal-process and technical translation; LawDroid supplies the chatbot technology and maintenance. Other courts and legal-aid organizations are offered implementation lessons, not evidence of profession-wide displacement or market restructuring. No staffing reductions, lawyer substitution or legal-fee effects are claimed.
